newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakhstan's rating seen better than Russia's.
newsitem.headline: Kazakhstan's rating seen better than Russia's.

text.p: Kazakhstan's sovereign debt ratings, expected within days, are likely to be better than those recently assigned to Russia, Western economists said on Wednesday.
Grigory Marchenko, deputy chairman of the National Bank of Kazakhstan, said the former Soviet republic's ratings would be announced within days.
"We expect them by the end of the week," he said.

Representatives of the big international rating agencies -- Standard & Poor's, Moody's and London-based IBCA -- visited Kazakhstan in September ahead of Almaty's planned debut Eurobond issue later this year.
"Kazakhstan should get a better rating than Russia," said one Western economist.
Kazakh officials say they are planning a $100 million three-year Eurobond issue in November or December, which will be lead-managed by ABN AMRO Hoare Govett.
The main aim of the Eurobond is to register a presence on international capital markets rather than raise funds.
The rating announcement will be followed by a road-show in London, New York and Tokyo, Marchenko said.
Earlier this month the three agencies gave high speculative ratings to Russia, which also plans to launch a Eurobond by the end of the year.
Moody's assigned Russia a better than expected Ba2 long-term rating, S&P gave it BB- and IBCA gave Russia BB+. These rank Russia below Hungary but above Brazil.
Although Russia might appear to be a stronger economy than Kazakhstan, the oil-rich Central Asian country has a number of points in its favour, the economists said.
One factor weighing against Russia in any rating is its large foreign debt, of about $120 billion.
Russia has assumed the foreign liabilities of the former Soviet Union, leaving other former republics like Kazakhstan with negligible foreign debt.

Russia's natural resources and regular trade surpluses mean it is well able to service the debt, but rescheduling deals with the London Club of commercial bank creditors, and the Paris Club of government creditors have not yet been formally closed.
Kazakhstan expects a small increase in gross domestic product this year, whereas Russia is resigned to a drop in GDP of about five percent and forecasts stagnant output next year.
Politically, Kazakhstan is perceived as more stable than Russia, with a more cohesive government team with a coherent vision of the future, the economists said.
Kazakhstan's main liability is its current inability to transport its oil, the basis of future wealth, to Western markets.
The Caspian Pipeline Consortium plans to link the Kazakh Tengiz oil field to Russia's Black Sea port near Novorossiisk via a $1.5 billion pipeline.
But other pipeline proposals are proceeding only slowly, holding up multi-billion dollar projects by Western energy majors in Kazakhstan.
However, the ratings assigned to the country will be on a medium or long-term basis, and will assume that the pipelines will be built, the economists said.
"These pipelines will happen, it's in everyone's interest," said one economist.
